13700: Repulse means to push something or someone away — but depending on the context, that "pushing away" can happen in three very different ways: physically, socially, or emotionally. Think of it as one word with three layers of meaning, all connected by the same idea of rejection and force.
Meaning 1: To Fight Off and Push Back (Physical / Military)

This is the oldest and most literal meaning. When an army, a group, or a person repulses an attack or an attacker, they successfully resist and drive them back by force.

The key idea here is not just blocking, but actively pushing the threat away.

Examples:

  • "The soldiers repulsed the enemy's charge and held the fort."
  • "The goalkeeper repulsed every attempt to score."
  • "The city repulsed three invasions before finally falling."

Think of it this way: if someone tries to knock down your door and you not only stop them but force them back into the street — you have repulsed them.
Meaning 2: To Coldly Reject or Rebuff (Social)

In a social or personal situation, to repulse someone means to firmly and often coldly turn them away — to refuse their request, their affection, or their attempt to get close to you.

This isn't a gentle "no, thank you." It carries a sense of deliberate, and sometimes harsh, rejection.

Examples:

  • "He tried to make conversation with her, but she repulsed him with a sharp glare."
  • "Every time he offered help, she repulsed him."
  • "The celebrity repulsed all attempts by the journalist to get an interview."

The person being repulsed here is left feeling shut out, rejected, and possibly embarrassed.
Meaning 3: To Cause Disgust or Strong Revulsion (Emotional / Sensory)

This is the most commonly used sense in modern, everyday English. When something repulses you, it causes you to feel intense disgust or revulsion — a powerful, almost physical reaction of "get this away from me."

Examples:

  • "The rotting smell from the bin repulsed her the moment she walked in."
  • "He was repulsed by the cruelty he witnessed."
  • "The graphic images repulsed the entire audience."

Notice that in this meaning, the subject (the thing doing the repulsing) is usually the cause of disgust — a smell, a sight, a behavior — and the object (the person being repulsed) is the one experiencing it.

All three meanings share the same invisible thread — forceful rejection:

  • In Meaning 1, it is a physical force that pushes something back.
  • In Meaning 2, it is a social force that pushes a person away.
  • In Meaning 3, it is an emotional/sensory force that makes you want to retreat from something.

You can think of repulse as the word you use when rejection isn't mild or neutral — it always involves some kind of strong, active pushing away, whether on a battlefield, in a conversation, or in your gut.

Repulse is a transitive verb, meaning it always needs an object — something or someone being repulsed. It cannot stand alone.

The most common patterns are:

  • [Someone] repulsed [an attack / an attacker] → Meaning 1
  • [Someone] repulsed [a person] → Meaning 2
  • [Something] repulsed [someone] → Meaning 3

Notice how Meaning 3 flips the typical sentence structure — the thing causing disgust is the subject, and the person feeling disgust is the object. This is similar to how the verbs "disgust," "horrify," and "nauseate" work.

You can also use it in the passive voice:

  • "She was repulsed by his behavior." (= His behavior repulsed her.)
  • "The attack was repulsed within hours."

Repulse vs. Repel:
These two are very close siblings. In fact, they are interchangeable in most situations. However, repel is more common in everyday speech, while repulse tends to feel slightly more formal, dramatic, or literary. If you're writing a novel about a battle or a deeply unpleasant experience, "repulse" carries more weight. In casual conversation, "repel" sounds more natural.

Repulse vs. Disgust:
"Disgust" is purely about the feeling of revulsion. "Repulse" carries that same emotional meaning but adds a layer of force — it doesn't just make you feel sick, it makes you want to actively turn away or retreat. "Repulse" is stronger and more visceral.

Repulse vs. Reject:
"Reject" is neutral and common. It simply means to say no to something. "Repulse," in its social meaning, implies a harsher, more cutting form of rejection — one that leaves the other person feeling pushed away, not just declined.

Repulse vs. Rebuff:
These are very similar in the social meaning. Both describe a sharp rejection. The difference is subtle: rebuff is almost always about rejecting a person's friendly or romantic approach, while repulse in the social sense can apply more broadly to any kind of advance, request, or effort.

The adjective repulsive describes something that causes disgust — "a repulsive smell," "repulsive behavior."

The past participle repulsed describes how a person feels after experiencing that disgust — "I was repulsed by the smell."

Both come from the same verb, but they describe different sides of the experience: the cause versus the reaction.

MeaningContextThe force involved
  • Push back physically → Used in battles, sports, and physical confrontations.
  • Reject someone socially → Used when someone is turned away coldly and firmly.
  • Cause disgust → Used when something triggers a powerful, gut-level aversion.

In all three cases, "repulse" is never a soft word. It always describes something forceful, sharp, and unambiguous. When something or someone is repulsed, there is no question about it — the rejection is complete.
13701: Repulsion is a noun. It refers to either a strong feeling of disgust and aversion, or a force that pushes things apart. These are its two main senses, and both are in common, serious use.
Sense 1: The Emotional Meaning (most common in everyday life)

Repulsion, in this sense, is what you feel when something strikes you as deeply disgusting, disturbing, or revolting — to the point where your whole body seems to react. It is not mere dislike. It is a powerful, often involuntary reaction that makes you want to look away, back off, or get as far away as possible from the source.

It can be triggered by something you see (a gruesome wound, a rotting animal), something you smell (a foul stench), something you hear (a graphic description of cruelty), something you touch (a slimy, unexpected texture), or even something you simply think about or imagine (a disturbing idea or act).

The key feature of repulsion is that it is visceral — meaning it doesn't just stay in your mind. It crawls into your body. People describe feeling their stomach turn, their skin crawl, their throat tighten, or a sudden urge to recoil. It is as though your body is saying no on behalf of your mind.

Repulsion can be directed at:

  • A physical thing — rotting food, a wound, an insect infestation
  • A person's behavior — cruelty, dishonesty, or moral corruption
  • An idea or act — violence, injustice, something you find deeply wrong
  • A situation — witnessing something deeply uncomfortable or horrifying

Example sentences:

  • She felt a wave of repulsion when she opened the container and found the food covered in mold.
  • The more he spoke, the more her initial admiration turned into quiet repulsion.
  • He couldn't hide his repulsion at the graphic images shown during the documentary.
  • There was a repulsion in her gut that told her something was deeply wrong.
Sense 2: The Scientific Meaning (physics and chemistry)

In science, repulsion is a force — specifically, the force that pushes two objects or particles away from each other. It is the opposite of attraction.

The clearest everyday example is magnets. If you hold two magnets with their same poles facing each other (north-north or south-south), they resist being pushed together. That resistance — that invisible force pushing them apart — is called magnetic repulsion.

Similarly, in electricity and chemistry: particles or charges that are alike (both positive, or both negative) push each other away. This is called electrostatic repulsion. This principle explains, among many things, why atoms don't collapse into each other and why physical objects feel solid when you touch them.

Example sentences:

  • The repulsion between the two north poles of the magnets was strong enough to feel through your fingers.
  • Electrostatic repulsion prevents like-charged ions from getting too close to each other.

In science, repulsion is a precise, measurable force. It has nothing to do with feelings — it is purely physical.

Understanding what a word feels like in use is as important as knowing its definition.

Repulsion is a strong word. You would not say you feel repulsion at mildly unpleasant things — a boring meal, an awkward conversation. It is reserved for things that provoke a sharp, powerful reaction. If something merely annoys you or makes you mildly uncomfortable, repulsion is too heavy a word.

Repulsion is often sudden. It tends to hit you in a moment, like a reflex. You don't slowly build up to repulsion the way you might slowly lose respect for someone. It often arrives all at once.

Repulsion is involuntary. You don't decide to feel repulsion. It happens to you. This is part of what makes it different from a calm, reasoned judgment like "I find this wrong." Repulsion is raw and immediate.
How Repulsion Differs from Similar Words

There are several words that share territory with repulsion, and knowing the differences will sharpen your understanding.

Disgust is very close to repulsion in meaning. The difference is subtle: disgust is broader and more flexible — you can feel disgust at someone's attitude or at a minor unpleasantness. Repulsion tends to be stronger and more visceral, implying a recoiling reaction. Some people use them interchangeably, and in many contexts they are effectively synonyms.

Revulsion is nearly identical to repulsion in the emotional sense. If anything, revulsion feels slightly more intense — a sudden, overwhelming surge. The two words are often used interchangeably, but revulsion feels a touch more dramatic and sudden.

Aversion is milder. An aversion is a strong dislike or avoidance — you might have an aversion to spicy food, loud noise, or crowded spaces. It doesn't necessarily imply the physical, gut-level reaction that repulsion does. Aversion is more about preference and avoidance; repulsion is about revulsion.

Distaste is much gentler still. Distaste is a mild, restrained feeling of discomfort or disapproval. You might feel distaste at a rude comment. You would feel repulsion at something deeply disturbing or disgusting.
The Related Forms of This Word

Knowing the other forms of a word helps you use it fluently.

  • Repulse (verb) — to cause repulsion in someone, or in science, to push something away. "The sight repulsed him." / "The magnetic force repulsed the other magnet."
  • Repulsive (adjective) — something that causes repulsion. "The smell was repulsive." / "He found her behavior repulsive."
  • Repulsed (adjective/past tense) — the state of having been affected by repulsion. "She was visibly repulsed by what she saw."

Repulsion means one of two things:

  1. Emotional: A strong, often visceral feeling of disgust and aversion — a powerful internal "no" that can be felt in the body, triggered by something deeply unpleasant, disturbing, or morally reprehensible.
  2. Scientific: A force that pushes two things apart, as seen in magnets with the same poles or particles with the same electrical charge.

The word is strong, precise, and serious. Use it when the reaction you are describing is not mere discomfort but something sharp, powerful, and difficult to ignore.
13702:
If something is repulsive, it causes a strong, almost physical feeling of disgust, revulsion, or extreme dislike — the kind of reaction that makes you want to turn away, back away, or escape from it entirely. It is not merely unpleasant. It is so deeply offensive to your senses or your sense of decency that your gut instinct is to reject it completely.

Think of it this way: when you encounter something repulsive, your whole body seems to react — you might wince, shudder, feel your stomach turn, or feel an urgent desire to get away. The reaction is involuntary and powerful.

"Repulsive" has two distinct meanings — one used in everyday life, and one used in science.

1. The Everyday Meaning (Far More Common)

This is the meaning you will encounter almost everywhere. Something repulsive produces an intense feeling of disgust or loathing. It deeply offends your senses — sight, smell, taste, hearing — or your moral sense of what is decent and acceptable.

Examples in sentences:

  • "The wound had a repulsive smell that made everyone step back."
  • "His cruel treatment of animals was repulsive to all who witnessed it."
  • "She found the idea of eating raw meat repulsive."
  • "The villain in the story was not just evil — he was utterly repulsive in his arrogance and cruelty."

Notice how in each case, the reaction is not mild. It is a full, strong rejection — emotional or physical or both.

2. The Scientific Meaning (Physics)

In physics, "repulsive" describes a force that pushes things apart. When two magnets face each other at the same poles (north-north or south-south), they push each other away. That pushing force is called a repulsive force. The same idea applies to electric charges — two like charges repel each other, so the force between them is repulsive.

Example: "The repulsive force between the two positively charged particles prevented them from touching."

This scientific meaning is actually the origin of the everyday meaning — both share the same root idea of pushing away. Something repulsive in everyday life pushes you away emotionally, just as a repulsive force pushes objects away physically.
What Can Be Described as Repulsive?

"Repulsive" is a very flexible adjective. It can describe:

A person's appearance — "The creature in the horror film had a repulsive, rotting face."

A smell or taste — "The repulsive stench of the swamp made it impossible to breathe normally."

A behavior or action — "Lying to a grieving widow for personal gain is repulsive."

An idea or attitude — "Many people find extreme hate speech repulsive."

A personality or character — "Despite his wealth, his selfishness made him repulsive as a person."

The common thread in all these uses is the same: a strong, instinctive feeling of "I cannot stand this. I need to get away from it."

"Repulsive" sits near the extreme end of the scale of negativity. To understand where it sits, consider this rough scale of intensity for describing something unpleasant:

Mildly unpleasant → Unpleasant → Disagreeable → Distasteful → Disgusting → Repulsive

"Repulsive" is among the strongest words on this scale. When you call something repulsive, you are saying that your reaction to it is one of deep, visceral rejection — not just mild discomfort.
How Is It Different from Similar Words?

Several words are close in meaning to "repulsive," but each has a slightly different shade.

Disgusting is probably the closest synonym. The two words are nearly interchangeable. However, "repulsive" carries a slightly stronger sense of wanting to physically pull away, while "disgusting" leans more toward moral or sensory outrage. In practice, most native speakers use them interchangeably.

Revolting is also very similar — perhaps equally strong. "The food was revolting" and "The food was repulsive" mean essentially the same thing.

Offensive is broader and milder. Something offensive might hurt your feelings, disrespect you, or cross a social boundary — but it doesn't necessarily make your stomach turn. Repulsive does.

Hideous usually refers specifically to appearance — something hideous is visually very ugly. Repulsive can refer to appearance, but it can also refer to smell, behavior, ideas, and personality.

Vile is similarly strong, but "vile" often carries a moral weight — vile acts are not just disgusting but wicked. Repulsive is more about the reaction it causes than the moral judgment itself.
Repulsive vs. Repelled — A Quick Note

The adjective "repulsive" describes the thing causing the reaction. The reaction itself — the feeling of being pushed away — is described by the verb "repel" or the adjective "repelled."

  • "The smell was repulsive." (The smell is the repulsive thing.)
  • "I was repelled by the smell." (I am the one who experienced the reaction.)

This is a small but important distinction when using the word correctly.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

When you call something repulsive, you are communicating something powerful. You are not just saying you dislike something — you are saying it provokes a strong, unwilling, near-instinctive reaction of rejection. This makes it a word with significant emotional force. Using it casually about small things (like a flavor you don't prefer) would be an exaggeration. It is best reserved for things that genuinely provoke a deep sense of disgust, revulsion, or moral outrage.

Repulsive means causing such a strong feeling of disgust or dislike that you instinctively want to turn away from it — whether the cause is something you see, smell, hear, taste, or witness in someone's behavior or character.
13703:
To repurpose something means to take an existing thing — which was originally made or used for one specific purpose — and use it for a different purpose instead.

The thing itself already exists. You are not creating something new from scratch. You are simply finding a new job for something that already has an old job.

An old wooden ladder is repurposed as a bookshelf.

The ladder was built to help you climb. Now it holds books. Same ladder, new purpose.

Three things happen when you repurpose something:

  1. Something already exists — an object, a space, a piece of content, a skill, etc.
  2. It had an original purpose — why it was made or how it was first used.
  3. You assign it a new, different purpose — you use it in a way it was not originally intended for.

The item may need minor changes to fit its new role, or it may need none at all. Either way, the focus is on the shift in purpose, not on how much the object changed physically.

Physical objects:

  • Old car tyres repurposed as garden planters.
  • Empty glass jars repurposed as storage containers for spices.
  • Worn-out jeans repurposed as shopping bags.
  • A shipping container repurposed as a small home.

Spaces and buildings:

  • An abandoned factory repurposed as an art gallery.
  • A church repurposed as a library.
  • A spare bedroom repurposed as a home office.

Content and media:

  • A written blog post repurposed as a podcast episode.
  • A presentation made for a conference repurposed as a YouTube video.
  • Research data repurposed for a magazine article.

Skills and knowledge:

  • A doctor's communication skills repurposed for a career in teaching.
  • A soldier's discipline and leadership repurposed in a corporate management role.
How to Use It in a Sentence

The most common patterns are:

  • "Repurpose X as Y" — stating both the old thing and the new use.
    "They repurposed the old warehouse as a co-working space."
  • "Repurpose X for Y" — stating the thing and what it is now used for.
    "She repurposed her old phone for use as a baby monitor."
  • "Repurpose X" — just mentioning the action without naming the new use explicitly.
    "Instead of throwing it away, he decided to repurpose the broken cabinet."

Understanding what a word doesn't mean often makes the actual meaning sharper.

Repurpose ≠ Reuse
Reuse simply means using something again — but for the same purpose. You reuse a shopping bag by using it again for shopping. You repurpose that bag when you use it to store toys or carry gym clothes. The key difference is whether the purpose changes.

Repurpose ≠ Recycle
When you recycle something, it is usually broken down into raw material and made into something completely new (like turning plastic bottles into polyester fabric). When you repurpose something, the item stays mostly intact — it is not broken down. It is simply given a new role in its current form.

Repurpose ≠ Restore
To restore something is to bring it back to its original state or use. If you restore an old radio, you fix it so it works as a radio again. If you repurpose it, you turn it into, say, a flower pot or a lamp — a completely different role.

Repurposing carries a tone of creativity, resourcefulness, and practicality. When someone repurposes something, there is often an implied cleverness — the ability to look at something and see potential in it beyond what it was originally made for.

It also carries a sense of not wasting. Instead of throwing something away, you find new value in it. This is why the word is especially common in conversations about sustainability, minimalism, environmental consciousness, and smart design.
Forms of the Word You Will Encounter

• repurpose — base verb: "I want to repurpose this old dresser."
  • repurposed — past tense or adjective: "They repurposed the space." / "a repurposed barn."
  • repurposing — present participle or gerund: "Repurposing old furniture is becoming popular."
  • repurposable — adjective (less common): "These containers are easily repurposable."

To repurpose something is to take an already-existing thing and deliberately use it for a different purpose than it was originally made or intended for — without necessarily destroying or fundamentally transforming it in the process.
13704:
When we say someone or something is reputable, we mean they are known and respected for being good, honest, and trustworthy — especially within a particular field or community.

The word lives and dies on one concept: reputation. A person's reputation is what other people generally think and say about them based on their consistent behavior over time. If that reputation is a good one — built on honesty, quality, and reliability — then that person or thing is reputable.

Think of it this way: reputable = having a reputation worth respecting.

For someone or something to earn the label reputable, three ingredients usually need to be present:

1. Consistency over time. A single good act doesn't make you reputable. Reputation is built slowly, through repeated trustworthy behavior. A doctor who has practiced ethically for 20 years is reputable. A new clinic that just opened — even if it seems fine — hasn't yet earned that word.

2. Recognition by others. Reputation is not self-declared. You don't decide you're reputable — other people, through their experience and word-of-mouth, decide it for you. If a car mechanic is reputable, it's because customers and the wider community recognize and vouch for their honesty.

3. Being good at what they do AND being honest about it. Reputable combines competence (they do their job well) with integrity (they behave honestly and ethically). A skilled surgeon who overcharges patients dishonestly would not be called reputable. A helpful, honest advisor who isn't very knowledgeable might also fall short. You generally need both.

Reputable can describe several kinds of things:

  • People — a reputable lawyer, a reputable scientist
  • Businesses/Organizations — a reputable company, a reputable charity
  • Publications or Sources — a reputable journal, a reputable news outlet
  • Institutions — a reputable university, a reputable hospital
  • Brands or Products — a reputable manufacturer

In every case, the meaning is the same: this entity has earned genuine trust and respect from the people who know about it.

Reputable is a moderately strong word. It is a solid, real compliment — but it isn't the highest possible praise. Here's a rough sense of the ladder:

  • Reputable → trustworthy, well-regarded, respected (solid and reliable)
  • Highly reputable → exceptionally well-regarded
  • Prestigious → at the top, often implying fame and elite status

So calling a school "reputable" means: you can trust this school; it's known for doing things right. Calling it "prestigious" would mean it's at the very top, possibly world-famous. Reputable is grounded and practical; prestigious is more glamorous.

Understanding what a word doesn't mean is just as important.

  • Reputable ≠ Famous. A small, little-known law firm in a small town can be reputable if the local community deeply trusts it. Fame and reputation are different things. Fame is about how many people know you. Reputation is about what they know you for.
  • Reputable ≠ Perfect. It doesn't mean flawless. A reputable company may still make occasional mistakes — what matters is that they handle things honestly and have a consistent track record of good behavior.
  • Reputable ≠ Expensive or fancy. A budget hotel can be reputable. An affordable plumber can be reputable. The word has nothing to do with price or appearance.

The direct opposite is disreputable — meaning having a bad reputation; known for dishonesty, poor quality, or unethical behavior. A disreputable lender, for example, might trick customers with hidden fees or dishonest contracts.

Other words that express the opposite: shady, untrustworthy, dubious, sketchy (informal).
Words Close in Meaning (and How They Differ)

• Credible — focuses specifically on being believable and trustworthy as a source of information. A credible witness. A reputable witness would carry the extra meaning of also being generally well-regarded.
  • Reliable — focuses on dependability. Your old car might be reliable (it always starts), but we wouldn't call a car "reputable." Reliable is about performance; reputable is about earned social standing.
  • Respectable — very close to reputable, but slightly broader. Respectable can describe behavior or appearance ("he dressed in a respectable manner"), while reputable almost always refers to an entity's standing in the eyes of a community.
  • Trustworthy — focuses purely on honesty and reliability in keeping trust. Reputable includes this, but also includes the element of being publicly known for it.
  • Established — describes something that has existed for a long time and is recognized. An established brand is often reputable, but "established" alone doesn't guarantee good ethics — it just means longevity.
How It's Used in Real Sentences

• "Before hiring a contractor, make sure they are reputable — ask for references and check online reviews."

Here, reputable means: known in the community for honest, quality work.

  • "She only cites reputable sources in her research papers."

Here, reputable means: academically recognized and trustworthy; not random blogs or unreliable websites.

  • "We chose a reputable adoption agency to ensure the process was handled ethically."

Here, reputable means: well-known for doing things the right way, with integrity.

  • "The investment firm had a reputable history of transparent dealings with its clients."

Here, reputable describes a track record of trustworthy behavior over time.

When someone calls a person or organization reputable, the tone is calm, grounded, and confident. It's not gushing praise — it's more like a dependable endorsement. If a friend tells you, "Go to that clinic — it's reputable," they're saying: you can trust them; I'm confident they'll treat you right. It's reassurance rooted in evidence.
Reputable means: genuinely trusted and well-regarded by others, because of a consistent record of honesty, quality, and ethical behavior.
13705:
Your reputation is what other people collectively think and say about you — the general opinion that exists about you in other people's minds, based on your past actions, behavior, and track record over time.

It is not what you think about yourself. It is not what one person thinks about you. It is the shared, common belief that a group of people hold about you — and that belief gets passed from person to person through talk, observation, and experience.

Imagine you live in a neighborhood. Over the years, you always keep your promises, you help others, and you are honest in your dealings. People talk. Word spreads. Eventually, nearly everyone in that neighborhood thinks of you as a reliable, trustworthy person. That shared opinion — that general image of you in the community's mind — is your reputation.

Now imagine the opposite: someone who regularly cheats, lies, and lets people down. The same process happens in reverse. People talk, and the community forms a shared negative opinion. That too is a reputation.

The key idea: reputation lives in other people's minds, not your own.

A reputation is built from:

  • Repeated actions — not one event, but a pattern. One kind act doesn't make you kind. A history of kind acts does.
  • What others observe — people form opinions based on what they see, hear, or experience from you.
  • What others say — once people form opinions, they share them. This is how a reputation spreads beyond those who know you directly.

This is important: a reputation is shaped by reality (what you actually do), but also by perception (what people believe you do). Sometimes these match perfectly. Sometimes they don't — a person can have a good reputation they don't deserve, or a bad one that is unfair.

A reputation is not always purely good or purely bad. It can be:

  • A good reputation — people generally think well of you: "She has a reputation for being fair and honest."
  • A bad reputation — people generally think poorly of you: "He has a reputation for being unreliable."
  • A mixed reputation — people hold conflicting views: "The restaurant has a reputation for amazing food but terrible service."
  • A strong/solid reputation — the opinion is well-established and hard to shake.
  • A damaged reputation — something happened that harmed the previously good opinion people held.
Who or What Can Have a Reputation

Reputation doesn't only apply to people. Any entity that acts in the world and is observed by others can have one:

  • A person — a politician, a teacher, a doctor, a neighbor.
  • A company or organization — "Apple has a reputation for sleek, well-designed products."
  • A place — "That city has a reputation for being expensive."
  • A product — "This brand has a reputation for lasting a long time."
  • A profession — "Lawyers sometimes have a reputation for being difficult to understand."
How It Is Used in Sentences

• "She worked hard to build her reputation as a skilled surgeon."
  • "His reputation suffered after the scandal."
  • "The school has a reputation for academic excellence."
  • "Don't risk your reputation for a small gain."
  • "He has a reputation for always being late."
  • "It took her years to repair her damaged reputation."

You will often see it paired with these words: build, earn, protect, damage, ruin, destroy, repair, lose, maintain, establish, have, gain.
A Critical Feature: It Takes Time, But Can Be Lost Quickly

One of the most important things to understand about reputation is its fragility and slowness.

  • It takes a long time to build. A strong reputation is the result of consistent behavior over months or years.
  • It can be destroyed very quickly. One serious mistake, scandal, or betrayal can erase years of goodwill.

This is why people say things like "Your reputation is your most valuable asset" or "It takes a lifetime to build a reputation and a moment to ruin it."
How Reputation Differs from Similar Words

Since you are a learner, it helps to know how reputation differs from words that feel similar:

  • Character is who you actually are on the inside — your values, morals, and principles. Reputation is what people think you are. A person of good character might have a bad reputation (if people misunderstand them), and someone with a good reputation might have poor character (if they are secretly dishonest). Character is internal; reputation is external.
  • Fame means many people know of you or have heard of you. It is about being widely known. Reputation is about what people think of you once they know of you. A famous person can have a bad reputation. The two are separate things.
  • Image is very similar to reputation, but image often implies something more deliberately constructed or managed — the picture someone tries to project. Reputation feels more like a natural accumulation of what others genuinely think. A politician might carefully manage their image, but their reputation is what the public actually believes about them underneath the management.
  • Prestige is a form of high reputation, specifically involving admiration, status, and respect in a particular field or social circle. It is a kind of reputation — a specifically high-status one.

At its deepest level, reputation is about social trust. Human society runs on trust — we need to know who to rely on, who to hire, who to do business with, who to befriend. Reputation is the system by which that information is stored and shared in a community. It is your social track record.

When someone says "Your reputation precedes you," they mean that people already know what to expect from you before you even arrive — your reputation has traveled ahead of you and introduced you before you could introduce yourself.

This is why reputation matters so much in professional life, social life, and business: it determines whether people will trust you, work with you, buy from you, or recommend you — often before they even meet you.
13706:
Repute means the opinion that people in general hold about someone or something — what a person, place, or organization is known for or thought to be like, in the eyes of others.

Think of it this way: your repute is not what you think of yourself. It is what the world thinks of you, based on what it has seen, heard, or come to believe over time.

A surgeon with decades of flawless work has a repute for precision and care.
A restaurant that has been serving bad food for years has a repute for poor quality.

In both cases, the repute did not come from one moment. It built up gradually, through the steady accumulation of how others experienced and talked about that person or place.
The Key Idea: It Lives in Other People's Minds

This is the single most important thing to understand about "repute." It does not live inside you — it lives outside you, in the minds of others. You can influence it through your actions, but you cannot simply declare it yourself. Other people decide it, hold it, and pass it on.

This is why a person can be wrongly accused and suffer a damaged repute — even if the truth is on their side, what others believe is what shapes repute.

Repute can lean in either direction:

Positive repute — being thought of well, with respect or admiration.

The university is of good repute and attracts students from across the world.
She is a writer of considerable repute in literary circles.

Negative repute — being thought of poorly, with suspicion or disapproval.

That neighborhood was once a place of ill repute, known for crime and disorder.
The company fell into bad repute after the scandal broke out.

"Of ill repute" is a particularly fixed and common phrase. You will encounter it often. It simply means: having a bad reputation, typically one associated with moral wrongdoing or disgraceful behavior. Historically, a "house of ill repute" was a polite way of saying a brothel.

This is one of the most useful and distinctive ways "repute" is used as a noun.

"By repute" means: according to what people generally say or believe, though not necessarily verified personally.

He is, by repute, the finest chess player in the country — though I have never seen him play myself.
The castle is, by repute, haunted.

Notice the slight distance in this phrase. When you say something "by repute," you are signaling that you are passing on the common belief — you are not personally vouching for it. It is like saying, "This is what people say." It can be true, it can be exaggerated, or it can even be a myth — but it is what repute holds.

• "of high repute" — greatly respected, held in very high regard.
  • "of some repute" — reasonably well known or respected, though not enormously famous.
  • "of international / national repute" — recognized and respected beyond a local circle, on a wider stage.
  • "held in high repute" — a slightly more formal way of saying someone is greatly respected.
  • "damage one's repute" — to harm the opinion others hold of someone.

Since you will certainly encounter both words, it is worth knowing how they relate.

They share the same core meaning. "Reputation" is the everyday, all-purpose word. "Repute" is the more formal, more literary version of the same idea. In casual speech and writing, people almost always use "reputation." "Repute," however, appears frequently in formal, legal, journalistic, or academic writing.

There is also a slight practical difference in how they appear in sentences:

  • "Reputation" is happy standing on its own: "She has a great reputation."
  • "Repute" tends to live more comfortably inside set phrases: "a doctor of good repute," "by repute," "of ill repute."

You would rarely say "She has a great repute" on its own — it sounds awkward. But "She is a doctor of great repute" sounds perfectly natural and elegant.
The Register: Who Uses This Word and When?

"Repute" is a formal word. You are more likely to read it than hear it in conversation. It appears in:

  • Legal language — "a person of good repute" in contracts or professional licensing
  • Journalism — describing public figures or institutions
  • Academic or professional writing — discussing organizations, experts, or establishments
  • Literature — especially older or more carefully crafted prose

If a friend calls you on the phone, they will almost certainly say "reputation," not "repute." But if you are reading a newspaper profile, a formal letter of recommendation, or a legal document, "repute" fits naturally.

"Repute" (noun) is the collective, general opinion that the world holds about a person, organization, or place — what they are known for, what they are believed to be, in the judgment of others. It is built over time, lives outside the person it describes, and can be positive or negative. As a noun, it appears most comfortably in fixed phrases like of good repute, of ill repute, and by repute. It is the formal, literary cousin of the everyday word "reputation," and it carries exactly the same essential meaning — just with a more refined, composed tone.
13707: To request means to ask for something — but not in the way you'd casually ask a friend. When you request something, you are asking politely and formally, while fully accepting that the other person may say yes or no. You are not forcing, demanding, or insisting. You are, in a sense, placing a polite appeal before someone who has the power to grant or deny it.
What makes it different from just "asking"

"Ask" is neutral and everyday. You ask a friend to pass the salt. You ask a child to be quiet.

"Request" carries more weight. It suggests:

  • Formality — you are in a professional, official, or respectful situation
  • Acknowledgment of the other person's authority — they can refuse, and you accept that
  • Deliberateness — you have thought about what you want and are putting it forward in a considered, respectful way

Think of it this way: a customer requests a refund. A passenger requests a window seat. A citizen requests access to government records. In each case, the person asking has no power to force the outcome — they are depending on goodwill, policy, or courtesy.
The power and politeness spectrum
It helps to see request on a scale alongside similar words:
Beg / Plead → Request → Ask → Demand → Command / Order

• Beg or plead: You are desperate. You are almost powerless. "Please, I'm begging you."
  • Request: Polite, formal. You respect the other person's right to say no.
  • Ask: Neutral, everyday, casual.
  • Demand: You feel strongly entitled. You are asserting pressure. Refusing is not really acceptable to you.
  • Command or order: You have authority over the person. Refusal is not an option.

Request sits in a dignified, respectful middle ground. It is firmer than begging, warmer and more polite than demanding.
How to use it in sentences (grammar patterns)
There are three main ways to use request as a verb:
1. Request + noun

The most straightforward pattern. You name the thing you want.

She requested a meeting with the manager.
He requested a refund.
They requested additional time to complete the project.
2. Request + that + sentence (using the subjunctive)

When you want to describe what you are asking someone to do, you use that followed by a verb in its base form (without to, and without -s for third person). This is called the subjunctive, and it is standard with request.

The doctor requested that the patient rest for a week. (not "rests")
She requested that the report be submitted by Monday. (not "is")
He requested that all staff attend the meeting.

Notice that the verb after that does not change for he/she/it. This is a rule specific to formal verbs like request, insist, suggest, recommend, and demand.
3. Request + person + to + verb

You can also name the person directly and tell them what you want them to do.

The officer requested the driver to step out of the vehicle.
She requested them to keep their voices down.

This pattern is a little more formal and direct — you are addressing a specific person with a specific action.
The passive voice — very common with "request"

You will often see request used in the passive form, especially in official notices, signs, invitations, and announcements. This form removes the focus from who is making the request and puts it on what is being asked.

Silence is requested in the library.
Your presence is requested at the annual gala.
Guests are requested to register at the front desk.
You are requested not to smoke on the premises.

This passive construction sounds very formal and authoritative, even impersonal — which is exactly why institutions, event organisers, and officials use it so often.
When to use request vs. when not to

Use request when:

  • You are writing or speaking formally — in emails, letters, official documents, announcements
  • The situation calls for politeness and professionalism
  • You want to show respect for the other person's position or authority
  • You are making a formal appeal — for information, permission, a service, or someone's time

Avoid request when:

  • You are speaking casually with a friend or family member ("I request that you pass me the remote" sounds stiff and odd)
  • You are speaking to someone clearly beneath your authority in a professional context — in that case, you would simply ask or instruct
Common combinations (what people typically request)

In real life, you will hear request paired with these things very often:

  • request a meeting / appointment
  • request information / details
  • request permission
  • request assistance / help
  • request a refund / replacement
  • request access (to a file, a building, a system)
  • request feedback
  • request time off (from work)
  • request a transfer
  • request documents / records
A note on tone and register

One subtle thing to understand: when you use request, you are signalling something about yourself and the situation. You are saying, "I am approaching this seriously and respectfully." This is why lawyers, diplomats, doctors, government officials, HR professionals, and business people use it constantly. It conveys that you mean what you say, that you are not being casual about it, and that you understand the other person has the right to respond as they see fit.

In contrast, overusing request in casual conversation can make you sound stiff, distant, or even a little cold. Good communication means matching your word choice to your context.
Summary in one sentence
To request is to formally and politely ask for something from someone who has the power to give or deny it, with the understanding that they are free to respond either way.
13708: A requiem is a solemn tribute to the dead — specifically, a prayer, ceremony, or piece of music offered for the peace and rest of a person's soul after they have died. The word always carries a mood of deep mourning, solemnity, and reverence. That is its emotional core. Everything else below is just that core idea appearing in different settings.

In the Catholic Church, a Requiem Mass (often simply called "a requiem") is a special church service held for someone who has died. It is not quite the same as a general funeral service. It is a specific, formal type of Mass — a sacred church ceremony — whose entire purpose is to pray for the soul of the deceased, asking God to grant them eternal rest and peace. The tone is deeply solemn and serious. It is not a cheerful "celebration of life"; it is a reverent, quiet act of prayer on behalf of the dead. This is where the word originates and where its meaning is purest.

Over the centuries, composers began writing large-scale music specifically designed to be sung during this Mass. This music itself came to be called "a requiem." So when someone says "Mozart wrote a requiem," they mean Mozart composed a major musical work — typically written for a choir, vocal soloists, and an orchestra — that was created to be performed during, or in the spirit of, a Mass for the dead.

Today, a requiem as a musical piece exists both as a religious work performed in a church and as a concert work performed in a concert hall. You don't need to be at a funeral to experience one. Some of the most celebrated requiems in history are Mozart's Requiem (which he left unfinished at the time of his death), Verdi's Requiem, Brahms' "A German Requiem," and Fauré's Requiem. Each composer brings a deeply personal voice to the form, which is why these pieces can sound remarkably different from one another — some are thunderous and dramatic, others are gentle and consoling — but they all share the same underlying purpose: to honor and mourn the dead through music.

Outside of religion and music, "requiem" is also used in a broader, metaphorical sense to describe anything — a speech, an article, a film, a final gesture — that acts as a last tribute or farewell to someone or something that is gone. It carries the same emotional weight as before: mourning, finality, and quiet respect.

For example: "The journalist's final article was a requiem for a way of life that had vanished." Or: "The closing ceremony felt like a requiem for everything the team had built together." Notice that in this figurative sense, the word doesn't have to refer to a person who has literally died. It can describe the end of an era, a place, a relationship, or an idea — anything that has permanently passed. What never changes is the feeling: something is gone, it mattered, and this moment honors that.
The One Thing That Never Changes

Across all three uses — religious, musical, and figurative — the word "requiem" always signals the same emotional register: something or someone has been lost, and what you are witnessing is a serious, careful, loving act of farewell. It is never a casual or lighthearted word. It belongs to the language of grief, memory, and deep respect. Whenever you encounter it, in any context, you can be sure the moment is a heavy one — something final is being acknowledged and honored.
13709:
Require means: something is necessary — it cannot be skipped, ignored, or avoided.

When you say something is "required," you are saying its absence causes a real problem. Either a task fails, a rule is broken, or survival is impossible without it. It is not a preference or a suggestion. It is a genuine necessity.
The Two Main Ways It's Used

1. Natural or Practical Necessity

Here, "require" describes what something needs in order to function, exist, or succeed. No person is demanding anything — the situation itself makes it necessary.

"Plants require sunlight."
(Without sunlight, they simply cannot survive.)

"This recipe requires three eggs."
(Without the eggs, the recipe won't work.)

"Climbing this mountain requires great physical fitness."
(You cannot do it without that fitness.)

Notice: the subject (plants, the recipe, climbing the mountain) is not a person giving orders. It's a situation, a task, or a living thing. The necessity comes from the nature of things, not from someone's will.

2. Obligation Imposed by Authority, Rules, or Law

Here, "require" describes what a person, institution, law, or rule demands — something you are obligated to do or provide. Someone with authority is insisting on it.

"The law requires all drivers to carry a licence."
(It is a legal obligation. You have no choice.)

"The school requires students to wear uniforms."
(The institution is imposing this rule.)

"The contract requires payment within 30 days."
(A legal agreement is binding you to this.)

"My boss requires a weekly progress report from me."
(A person in authority is demanding this.)

Notice: the subject here is an authority — a law, an institution, a contract, a person in power. The necessity comes from their rules or demands.
The Crucial Shared Thread

Both uses share one thing: what is required is not optional.

  • In the first use — it's not optional because reality makes it impossible without it.
  • In the second use — it's not optional because breaking the rule has consequences (punishment, failure, legal trouble).

This is what makes "require" stronger and more serious than many other words.
Who or What Can "Require" Something?

Almost anything can be the subject of "require":

  • A task or activity: "The job requires five years of experience."
  • A place or institution: "The hospital requires visitors to register."
  • A situation: "The crisis requires immediate attention."
  • A law or rule: "The regulation requires safety helmets on the site."
  • A formal/official person: "The judge requires your presence in court."
  • A living thing: "The human body requires sleep."
How to Use It in a Sentence (Grammar Patterns)

Pattern 1: require + noun

"This work requires patience."
"The task requires complete silence."

Pattern 2: require + object + to + verb
(Someone requires a person to do something)

"The manager requires all staff to sign in."
"The form requires you to provide your address."

Pattern 3: require + that + clause (more formal)

"The rules require that all phones be switched off."
"The policy requires that employees declare any conflicts."

Pattern 4: require + verb-ing

"The project requires testing every component."
"The job requires travelling frequently."
"Required" — the Adjective Form

When something is described as "required," it means it is compulsory or necessary — not optional.

"Attendance is required." (You must attend.)
"A signature is required." (You must sign.)
"These are the required documents." (You must have these.)
How "Require" Compares to Similar Words

Understanding where "require" sits among similar words sharpens your sense of it greatly.

Require vs. Want
"Want" is a desire — you can live without it. "Require" is a necessity — you cannot proceed without it.

"I want a bigger office." (desire, optional)
"The machine requires a power source." (necessity, non-negotiable)

Require vs. Need
These are very close in meaning. The key difference is tone. "Need" is neutral and everyday. "Require" is more formal, more precise, and often carries a sense of authority or structure.

"I need help." (casual, personal)
"The process requires authorisation from two managers." (formal, procedural)

Require vs. Request
A "request" is an asking — the other person can say no. "Require" is a necessity or demand — there is no real option to decline.

"I request your feedback." (polite asking; you may choose)
"The visa requires a bank statement." (you must provide it; there is no option)

Require vs. Demand
Both involve insisting, but "demand" is more aggressive and emotional — it often implies impatience or confrontation. "Require" is more formal and neutral — it describes a rule, a system, a law, or a calm authority.

"He demanded an apology." (forceful, emotional, personal)
"The application requires proof of identity." (formal, impersonal, structured)
The Passive Voice: "Required to"

You will very often see "require" used in the passive form: "is/are required to." This is extremely common in formal, legal, and official language.

"You are required to submit your documents by Monday."
"All passengers are required to fasten their seatbelts."
"Employees are required to complete the training."

This passive form puts the focus on the obligation itself, not on who is imposing it. It sounds official and impersonal — like a rule that exists above any individual.
Subtle Nuance: Require Implies Genuine Necessity

There is an important subtlety. "Require" implies that if the required thing is absent, something genuinely goes wrong — not just inconveniently, but fundamentally.

"Success requires hard work."

This doesn't mean hard work is merely helpful. It means without hard work, success is not fully possible.

"The job requires a degree."

This means without the degree, you are disqualified — not just disadvantaged.

This sense of genuine, non-trivial necessity is what gives "require" its weight and seriousness.
A Few More Natural Examples in Context

• "Good writing requires clarity of thought." — clarity is a true necessity for good writing.
  • "The experiment requires precise measurements." — without precision, the experiment is compromised.
  • "Your visa requires a valid passport." — no passport, no visa. Full stop.
  • "Running a business requires both skill and patience." — both are genuinely needed, not just helpful.
  • "The position requires fluency in two languages." — it is a mandatory condition of the role.
  • "The medicine requires a doctor's prescription." — you legally cannot get it without one.
Summary

Require means: something is a genuine necessity — it must be present or done, and its absence leads to failure, impossibility, or violation of a rule. It is used both when nature/reality makes something necessary, and when a rule, law, or authority imposes an obligation. It is more formal than "need," stronger than "want," calmer than "demand," and more binding than "request." What is required is never optional.
